questions.topic: ANN Index Types by Operational Profile
questions.question: What is the central tradeoff in approximate nearest-neighbor search?
options: Scanning every stored vector so that exactness is raised above the baseline
Giving up some exact recall in exchange for less search work and lower latency
Spending more memory on graph edges so that index build time stays short
Accepting a slower build so that every query returns the exact top k

questions.topic: ANN Index Types by Operational Profile
questions.question: How does HNSW organize vectors?
options: As a set of coarse centroids with each vector assigned to its nearest one
As a relational join table linking each vector to its k nearest neighbors
As one sorted list ordered by distance from the corpus centroid
As a multilayer proximity graph navigated from sparse upper layers down

questions.topic: ANN Index Types by Operational Profile
questions.question: An IVF index has 10,000 lists and nprobe is 20. What fraction of lists is probed?
options: 20 percent
2 percent
0.2 percent
0.02 percent

questions.topic: ANN Index Types by Operational Profile
questions.question: What is the primary purpose of product quantization?
options: To compress vectors into short codes so that search and storage cost less
To make distance computations exact by storing full-precision residuals
To remove the training step that an inverted-file index would otherwise need
To store the original source text beside each vector for cheap reranking

questions.topic: ANN Index Types by Operational Profile
questions.question: Why can an HNSW index with heavy churn need maintenance or rebuilding?
options: Because HNSW rejects insertions once its upper layers have been constructed
Because graph indexes hold their edges on disk and never consume any memory
Because tombstones and incremental edits degrade the graph and waste its memory
Because each delete forces the embedding model to be retrained on the corpus

questions.topic: ANN Index Types by Operational Profile
questions.question: What is the strongest reason to retain a flat exact implementation?
options: It always answers with lower latency than any approximate index structure
It gives a recall reference that separates ANN loss from embedding quality
It removes the need to store vectors, since distances are computed on text
It substitutes for the availability tests that a production index would require

questions.topic: Keeping the Vector Store in Sync with the Source of Truth
questions.question: What should be authoritative for vector records?
options: The proximity graph the ANN index has built over the current generation
The query log, whose recent hits show which records are actually in use
The search result cache, which holds the most recently served documents
The source corpus or feature catalog the projection is derived from

questions.topic: Keeping the Vector Store in Sync with the Source of Truth
questions.question: What is safer than direct dual-writing to the source and vector store?
options: Committing the source first, then projecting it through an outbox or CDC stream
Writing the vector store first and continuing even if the source write fails
Retrying each of the two writes with random backoff until both have landed
Skipping both writes until a nightly reconciliation job can apply them safely

questions.topic: Keeping the Vector Store in Sync with the Source of Truth
questions.question: How should a vector projection handle a redelivered change event?
options: Write a new record under a fresh identifier so no earlier state is lost
Upsert the deterministic record and its source version idempotently
Reject it outright, since a redelivered event always carries stale content
Queue it for the next full rebuild rather than applying it to the live index

questions.topic: Keeping the Vector Store in Sync with the Source of Truth
questions.question: Why does count-only reconciliation miss some defects?
options: Because index record counts cannot be computed without a full table scan
Because reconciliation reads the index alone and never a source manifest
Because one missing record and one orphan cancel out in the overall total
Because every vector record shares one identifier across index generations

questions.topic: Keeping the Vector Store in Sync with the Source of Truth
questions.question: Why can permission revocation require a stricter path than ordinary indexing freshness?
options: Because continued access is a security failure that may need an immediate fail-closed check
Because a revocation event changes the dimension the affected vectors were built at
Because newly published content is always private until it is explicitly shared
Because vector indexes cannot store the metadata that a permission check reads

questions.topic: Keeping the Vector Store in Sync with the Source of Truth
questions.question: What should a complete index-generation manifest identify?
options: The index name and the alias that currently points at the ready generation
The record count reached at build time and the time the build finished
The distance metric and the vector dimension that the collection was created with
The corpus snapshot, model, expected IDs, filters, parameters, and validation

questions.topic: When You Do Not Need a Vector Database
questions.question: When is flat exact search a strong first choice?
options: When recall is irrelevant because results are only used for rough browsing
When the collection and query rate fit the compute and the latency budget
When no filters can be expressed against the metadata stored per vector
When the corpus contains no vectors and only lexical fields are searchable

questions.topic: When You Do Not Need a Vector Database
questions.question: Why might an existing relational or search database be preferable?
options: It may already provide transactions, filters, joins, and adequate vector search
It produces embeddings of higher quality than a dedicated vector service does
It removes the need to evaluate relevance because its ranking is already tuned
It stores no metadata, so security review has a much smaller surface to check

questions.topic: When You Do Not Need a Vector Database
questions.question: About how much raw float32 storage do 100,000 vectors of dimension 384 require before metadata?
options: 15.4 megabytes
1.54 gigabytes
154 megabytes
15.4 gigabytes

questions.topic: When You Do Not Need a Vector Database
questions.question: What is a good design for related items when all query items are known in advance?
options: Re-embed each catalog item on every request so neighbors reflect fresh text
Run an online ANN query per request, which is mandatory once vectors exist
Crawl external sources at request time to widen the candidate neighbor pool
Precompute the neighbors offline and store the top IDs in a key-value table

questions.topic: When You Do Not Need a Vector Database
questions.question: What evidence justifies moving from exact search to ANN?
options: Measured scale or latency pressure the exact baseline cannot meet
A vendor benchmark showing high recall on a public embedding dataset
The team has produced its first batch of embeddings for the corpus
A plan to expand the platform team's infrastructure responsibilities

questions.topic: When You Do Not Need a Vector Database
questions.question: How can a team reduce vector-database exit cost?
options: Store the vectors only in the vendor's private on-disk index format
Spread the vendor's client API calls throughout all application modules
Keep open authoritative vectors and metadata behind a narrow interface
Discard model versions once the current index generation is serving
